mcqs.question: Why is O(log n) considered a meaningful memory budget for class L, rather than an arbitrary small number?
options: Because log n space is enough to store a full copy of any input of size n
Because log n space guarantees the algorithm also runs in constant time
Because log n bits is exactly enough to store a constant number of pointers/indices into an input of size n, without room to copy the input itself
Because it's simply the smallest space bound anyone has studied
mcqs.explanation: An index into an array of n elements needs about log n bits to represent, so O(log n) space allows a constant number of such pointers/counters — enough to track position while scanning input — but not enough to store a copy of the input, which would need O(n) space. This is exactly why L-class algorithms are structured around scanning with pointers rather than building auxiliary data structures the size of the input.

mcqs.question: We know L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE. What is the current state of knowledge about whether any of these are STRICT subset relationships?
options: All of them have been proven strict
None of the containments are proven strict anywhere in the chain
It has been proven that all five classes are actually equal
Every containment except L ⊂ PSPACE (the endpoints) remains open; L is proven strictly smaller than PSPACE via the space hierarchy theorem
mcqs.explanation: The space hierarchy theorem proves L ⊂ PSPACE is strict (more space provably allows solving more problems), but the intermediate boundaries — including the famous P vs NP question — remain unresolved open problems. It's neither the case that everything is proven strict nor that everything is proven equal; it's a specific, known exception (the endpoints) amid broad open questions in the middle.

mcqs.question: TQBF (true quantified boolean formula) is PSPACE-complete, playing the same role for PSPACE that 3-SAT plays for NP. Why does two-player game analysis (like generalized geography) naturally land in PSPACE rather than NP?
options: Because games are always harder than any NP-complete problem
Because generalized geography has no known complete algorithm at all

Because alternating quantifiers (exists/forall) in TQBF mirror alternating turns between two players, so reasoning about optimal play under alternating turns is structurally the same problem as evaluating an alternating-quantifier formula
Because NP only applies to single-player decision problems, never two-player games
mcqs.explanation: TQBF's alternating exists/forall quantifiers directly mirror a two-player game's alternating turns — 'exists a move such that for all opponent responses...' is exactly the structure of reasoning about optimal play, which is why PSPACE-complete games generalize the single quantifier structure of NP-complete problems like 3-SAT (which only has 'exists'). It's not that games are unconditionally harder than every NP problem, and generalized geography does have a known (PSPACE) algorithm; the class distinction comes from quantifier structure, not an arbitrary NP/game split.

mcqs.question: Minimax search with alpha-beta pruning explores an exponentially large game tree but only ever holds one root-to-current-node path in memory. Which complexity-class signature does this match?
options: PSPACE's actual signature: exponential time is common for PSPACE-complete problems, while the defining resource bound — space — stays polynomial (even linear here), the opposite of assuming space and time hardness always move together
This algorithm proves PSPACE equals P, since it runs efficiently in practice
This is impossible; any exponential-time algorithm must also use exponential space
This shows alpha-beta pruning solves an NP-hard problem in polynomial time
mcqs.explanation: PSPACE-hardness describes a polynomial space bound with (typically) no known polynomial-time algorithm — exactly what minimax with alpha-beta demonstrates concretely: the search tree is exponential in time to explore, but the memory footprint stays proportional to the tree's depth (linear), not its size. Time and space complexity are independent axes; an algorithm can absolutely be exponential in time while staying polynomial (or better) in space, and this says nothing about P vs PSPACE or NP-hardness.
